Newborn Care

Plantago herbs while breastfeeding: plant identity, evidence and safer choices

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Plantago herbs have a long history of traditional use, but a familiar name does not identify a safe breastfeeding treatment. Species, plant part and preparation matter. A broad-leaved plantain remedy, a ribwort leaf extract and a labelled ispaghula laxative are not interchangeable. Limited information about a herb also does not prove either safety or harm. Check the actual product and the reason for using it before relying on it for yourself or your baby.

Start with the plant and the exact preparation

Plantago is a genus containing different plants. Broadleaf or common plantain, Plantago major, has a low rosette of broad oval leaves and upright, leafless flower spikes; ribwort plantain is Plantago lanceolata. The everyday name plantain can also mean an unrelated banana-like cooking fruit. A common name, leaf description or photograph cannot reliably identify a collected herb or certify that it is safe to use.

A product called barhang or plantain may not specify a Latin species. Do not assume it is definitely P. major or that evidence for another Plantago species applies. Roots, leaves, flowers, seeds, teas, juices and concentrated extracts can have different constituents and effects. Vitamins, minerals, mucilage, fibre or flavonoids in plant material do not make all these preparations equivalent to psyllium. Avoid roadside or waste-ground collection and do not use an image as a foraging guide.

Traditional uses are not proof of clinical benefit

Claims for Plantago include fever relief, throat or tonsil irritation, hoarseness, dry cough, mucus and lung irritation, asthma and tuberculosis symptoms. Other claims concern skin repair, eczema, itching, swelling, bruises, wound disinfection or pulling out infection; dental or ear pain and chemotherapy-related mouth inflammation are also mentioned. These are different conditions, not one established treatment. Laboratory findings or longstanding use do not show that a home preparation cures infection or is suitable during breastfeeding. Do not replace inhalers, antibiotics, dental care or the cancer team's mouth-care plan.

Digestive claims include constipation, irritable bowel symptoms, gastritis, ulcerative colitis, stomach-lining repair, cramps and bloody diarrhoea. Further claims involve liver or kidney function, bladder inflammation, diuresis, blood cleansing, pain relief, jaundice, diabetic foot wounds and heavy or irregular menstrual bleeding. There is no basis here for promising these outcomes from an unspecified Plantago remedy. Snakebite and seizures need appropriate emergency or established medical care, not a plant intended to draw out venom or treat epilepsy. Adult use also does not demonstrate benefit for infant gut spasms or through breast milk.

Breastfeeding evidence is specific, not transferable between herbs

Information about medicinal broadleaf Plantago preparations during breastfeeding is insufficient to establish a safe dose, milk transfer, infant effects or a benefit to milk supply. Neither no reported problem nor an amount called moderate certifies safety. Do not assume all adult traditional benefits occur in a breastfeeding parent or reach a baby through milk. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about a better-studied treatment for the actual symptom before using a tea, mixed-seed product or extract.

For comparison, the European Medicines Agency's 2025 monograph concerns particular P. lanceolata leaf preparations and traditional uses for mouth or throat irritation, cough and minor skin inflammation. Its indications rely on longstanding use, and it does not recommend those preparations during pregnancy or lactation because safety data are insufficient. This is not a clinical approval of P. major, evidence of proven milk toxicity, or a reason to reject every medicine made from a Plantago species. Pregnancy and breastfeeding need separate assessment, including if you become pregnant while feeding.

Psyllium or ispaghula husk is a different product

Ispaghula husk is the seed coat of Plantago ovata and is used in defined bulk-forming laxative preparations. It is not the same as an unspecified broadleaf plantain tea or an assortment of whole seeds. NHS advice updated in 2026 permits a labelled ispaghula product during breastfeeding; LactMed and NHS specialist guidance explain that psyllium is not absorbed from the gut, so exposure through milk is not expected. That reasoning applies to the fibre preparation, not every chemical in leaves, roots or extracts.

If constipation is the reason for considering a herb, ask for an ingredient-specific plan rather than replacing an appropriate laxative with an uncertain remedy or abandoning treatment. Specialist breastfeeding recommendations generally concern healthy full-term infants; a premature or unwell baby, several medicines or a complex health history need individual advice. Follow the labelled product's fluid, swallowing and medicine-timing instructions. Suitability for the parent does not mean the same product or adult regimen can be given directly to a baby.

Read adverse-effect lists in the context of the product

Gas, bloating, cramps, nausea, diarrhoea or other digestive symptoms may have several causes. Bulk-forming husks can cause wind and bloating; inadequate liquid, swallowing difficulty or an existing narrowing or blockage can make them inappropriate or dangerous. Do not swallow a dry powder or use an unknown seed mixture as though it were a correctly labelled medicine. Abdominal pain with vomiting or marked swelling needs assessment rather than another fibre dose. A botanical name alone does not identify the relevant risk.

Allergy is possible, including to a husk powder; avoid inhaling powder and do not deliberately retry a product after a suspected reaction without advice. Claims that every Plantago preparation causes low blood pressure, uterine contractions, miscarriage or premature birth are not established by the evidence reviewed here. Equally, lack of data does not guarantee no side effects at a moderate amount. Pregnancy concerns should be discussed separately instead of treating every alleged pregnancy effect as a demonstrated harm to a breastfeeding infant.

Check interactions rather than changing prescribed medicines

Bring the exact ingredient list and all your medicines and supplements to the pharmacist. Some fibre products can change the absorption of other medicines; the timing needs to follow the specific label and pharmacy advice. Medicines for epilepsy, heart conditions, diabetes or thyroid disease may need particular review. An unspecified herb and a defined husk preparation can have different interaction profiles; do not apply one universal spacing rule or adjust an insulin, thyroid or other dose yourself.

A claim about vitamin K in a plant does not by itself prove that every Plantago product interacts with every blood thinner. If you take warfarin or another anticoagulant, discuss the proposed product rather than stopping treatment or relying on a generic herb list. Mixtures may include additional active ingredients, and product quality and concentration can vary. Ask before combining laxatives or adding another medicinal herb, and tell the team if you are pregnant as well as breastfeeding.

Do not turn a maternal herb into an infant or wound treatment

There is no demonstrated basis here for giving Plantago tea, leaves or seeds to a baby for cramps, feeding problems, jaundice or breathing symptoms, or for expecting a mother's remedy to treat them through milk. Do not put home plant preparations on nipples, in the infant's mouth or on an open or infected wound. A traditional label does not establish cleanliness, correct identity or an appropriate infant treatment. Ask the baby's clinician or feeding team about symptoms and effective care.

Suspected jaundice needs clinical advice, not a herb trial. A baby older than 24 hours with yellow eyes or skin needs urgent assessment; jaundice within the first 24 hours, or with difficulty waking, poor feeding, breathing difficulty, floppiness, abnormal movements, no wet nappies, or a temperature of 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower needs immediate emergency care. Yellow eyes or skin in the parent also needs urgent advice. A new diabetic foot wound should be reported promptly to the foot-care service; fever, spreading serious infection or threatened tissue requires emergency care rather than a leaf dressing.

If you already used a product, seek advice with useful details

A previous dose alone does not establish that your baby was harmed, but an unidentified preparation cannot be certified safe from the name. Keep the packaging or a clear ingredient list and note the amount, timing, route and any symptoms. Tell the clinician your baby's age, gestation at birth, feeding and health, plus your own conditions and medicines. Do not automatically stop necessary treatment or interrupt breastfeeding without a product-specific plan; urgent symptoms take priority over waiting for advice about routine feeding.

Seek review for persistent cough or fever, dental or ear pain, a painful skin lesion, urinary symptoms, ongoing digestive problems or unexplained bleeding instead of repeating an herbal course. Blood in stool, new jaundice or a worsening wound needs timely assessment. If you or the baby develops a suspected reaction, stop the unprescribed suspect product and ask for advice; severe symptoms require emergency services. Symptoms after a herb do not prove the herb caused them, but they still deserve appropriate care.

Recognise emergencies and avoid a remedy delay

Call emergency services for trouble breathing or swallowing, sudden tongue or throat swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, chest symptoms or severe illness. For suspected anaphylaxis, use a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector if available and do not wait for a rash. Suspected snakebite needs immediate emergency assessment; do not apply a herb, cut or suck the wound. A first seizure, one longer than usual or over five minutes when the usual duration is unknown, repeated seizures without recovery or breathing problems needs emergency help. Follow an established epilepsy emergency plan if trained, and never put a remedy, food or drink in the person's mouth during a seizure.

Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain worsened by movement or touch, or pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, faintness, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding needs immediate emergency care. Heavy bleeding after birth, particularly soaking a pad in an hour or passing very large clots, also needs immediate medical care; do not use an herb to stop it. During pregnancy or the year after birth, fever, persistent severe headache, vision changes or vomiting that prevents fluids staying down warrants immediate medical advice. Tell the team about pregnancy or a recent birth, and do not wait for a plant preparation to work.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Check the Latin name, plant part and all ingredients; distinguish a Plantago herbal remedy from a labelled psyllium husk medicine and avoid wild-plant identification by photograph.

Ask a pharmacist about the symptom, product, other medicines and baby's age and health before use; keep prescribed care and do not give an adult herb regimen to the baby.

Keep packaging after an exposure or suspected reaction and follow urgent warning signs immediately instead of waiting for an herbal treatment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record product names, plant parts, ingredients, timing and symptoms and prepare questions for a pharmacist or feeding team. It cannot identify a plant, certify product purity or breastfeeding safety, measure milk exposure, diagnose an infant's symptoms, choose a laxative or decide that emergency care can wait.

When to seek help

Call emergency services for breathing or swallowing difficulty, sudden tongue or throat swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness, confusion, chest symptoms, a first or prolonged seizure, repeated seizures without recovery, suspected snakebite, or severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain. Pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, faintness, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding also needs emergency care. Use prescribed adrenaline for suspected anaphylaxis without waiting for a rash; never put herbs or drinks in the mouth during a seizure or use a plant to draw out venom. Heavy postpartum bleeding needs immediate care. Newborn jaundice in the first 24 hours or with poor feeding, difficulty waking, abnormal temperature or breathing needs emergency assessment; other suspected jaundice needs urgent advice. Seek immediate medical advice for postpartum fever, severe persistent headache, visual changes or inability to keep fluids down. Do not substitute herbs for prescribed treatment, apply homemade remedies to nipples or wounds, or give them directly to a baby.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Plantago species and plant parts differ; a familiar name or image cannot identify a safe breastfeeding preparation.
  • Traditional respiratory, wound, digestive, bleeding and infant claims are not established benefits of an unspecified herb.
  • Defined psyllium or ispaghula husk can be compatible with breastfeeding, but that evidence does not extend to leaf teas or extracts.
  • Check allergies, swallowing and fluid needs, other medicines and the baby's health with a pharmacist; do not improvise treatment or give a maternal product to an infant.
  • Breathing problems, loss of consciousness, seizures, snakebite, serious pain, jaundice or heavy bleeding need appropriate urgent or emergency care, not a herbal trial.

Frequently asked questions

What are Plantago's traditional uses?

Claims include fever, throat and cough symptoms, skin or wound care, digestion, liver or kidney problems and bleeding. Some specified products have traditional-use indications, but that does not establish clinical benefit for every preparation or safety while breastfeeding. It is not a substitute for treating seizures, snakebite, tuberculosis or a serious wound.

Is medicinal Plantago safe while breastfeeding?

There is insufficient information to certify an unspecified leaf, root, seed mix, tea or extract as safe or set a lactation dose. Ask about the exact product and a better-studied treatment. Safety advice for a labelled psyllium husk laxative is separate.

What side effects can occur?

Risks depend on species, preparation, amount and health. Fibre husks may cause wind or bloating and can be unsuitable with swallowing difficulty or a suspected blockage; allergy is possible. A generic list of miscarriage, premature birth or low blood pressure does not establish these effects for every Plantago product or a breastfed infant.

Does it benefit a breastfed baby's digestion or jaundice?

That is not established. Do not give the baby a home herb preparation or expect a maternal dose to treat symptoms through milk. Suspected jaundice needs urgent advice, and jaundice in the first 24 hours or with poor feeding, difficulty waking or other serious symptoms needs emergency care.

Is plantain the same as a cooking banana?

No. Plantago herbs, such as broadleaf or ribwort plantain, differ from the fruit sometimes called plantain. A cooking-fruit discussion cannot establish the breastfeeding safety of a medicinal Plantago preparation.

Can I use prescribed ispaghula for constipation?

A defined ispaghula husk product can be used while breastfeeding when suitable for your symptoms and health. Check the exact label and pharmacist's advice, especially with a premature or unwell baby. That does not make an unidentified whole-seed or leaf remedy equivalent, or authorize giving the product to the baby.

What if I take a blood thinner or another medicine?

Show the exact product and full medicine list to a pharmacist. Fibre can affect absorption and a mixture may have other interactions. Do not stop anticoagulants, change other prescribed doses or apply a universal timing interval yourself.

What should I do after a suspected reaction?

Stop an unprescribed suspect product and seek advice with the packaging and timing. Breathing or throat difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness, severe or worsening pain, heavy bleeding or a seriously unwell baby needs emergency help. A previous dose without symptoms is not proof of harm; ask for a product-specific feeding and care plan rather than automatically stopping breastfeeding.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
